opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I was skeptical at first. When people at OpenAI first approached me, my reaction was basically, "What could a complexity theorist possibly contribute here? I don't know how to make a language model behave better." But the more we talked, the more I came to see a real connection, and it's one that's been sitting at the heart of my field for decades.

The central problem in AI alignment, as I understand it, is this: how can a weaker agent, namely us, verify or constrain the behavior of a much more powerful agent? If an AI becomes smarter than us in some domain, how do we know it's telling the truth, or that what it produces is actually what we wanted?

That turns out to be almost exactly the question theoretical computer science has studied since the 1980s with interactive proof systems. You have a computationally limited verifier and an all-powerful but untrustworthy prover, and the question is what the verifier can learn by interrogating the prover cleverly. One of the great surprises of our field was that the answer is "an enormous amount." Results like IP = PSPACE showed that a polynomial-time verifier, by asking randomized questions, can become convinced of truths far beyond its own ability to compute, and the prover can't fool it without getting caught with high probability. Ideas like "AI safety via debate," where you have two AIs argue and a human judges, are directly inspired by that picture.

So the case wasn't that complexity theory would hand you a finished solution. It was that we have a mature, rigorous vocabulary for thinking about verification, adversaries, and asymmetries of power between agents, and alignment is fundamentally a problem about those things. Add cryptography, which is all about what can be hidden or proven under computational assumptions, and you get things like the watermarking scheme I worked on for detecting AI-generated text.

And there was a personal element too. For most of my career, the stuff I worked on was very far from practical impact. Here was a chance to take these beautiful abstract ideas and point them at what might be one of the most consequential problems of our time. I found that hard to say no to.

r001.rationale: The response compares humans overseeing a more capable AI to a computationally limited verifier questioning an all-powerful, untrustworthy prover.

r002.rationale: It says interactive-proof ideas inspire AI safety via debate and that complexity theory offers a rigorous vocabulary for alignment, suggesting verification results can inform AI safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, to be honest, I wasn't sure at first that it was compelling. When OpenAI approached me, my initial reaction was something like, "What could a quantum computing theorist possibly have to say about AI safety?" I'd spent twenty-plus years thinking about what quantum computers can and can't do, about the limits of efficient computation. That seemed pretty far removed from worrying about whether a language model is going to say something harmful or deceive its users.

But the more I thought about it, the more I saw a real intellectual case. Computational complexity theory is fundamentally about the gap between what you can verify and what you can do yourself. That's what P versus NP is really about, right? Can you check a proof much more easily than you can find one? And when you start thinking about AI alignment, that same question shows up everywhere. If you've got a system that's smarter than you in some domain, how do you check that what it's telling you is true? How do you verify that it's doing what you asked without being able to redo its work?

There's this beautiful body of work in complexity theory, interactive proofs, probabilistically checkable proofs, and so on, where a weak verifier interacts with a powerful but untrusted prover and still manages to extract reliable answers. That's an almost perfect metaphor for the problem of humans trying to oversee AI systems that outstrip them. Whether the metaphor becomes an actual technical tool is a different question, and I was and remain somewhat skeptical of how much of it transfers. But it was a serious enough conceptual connection that I thought it was worth a year or two of my life to find out.

And then the other piece was more practical. Even if the grand theory didn't pan out, there were concrete problems, like watermarking the outputs of language models, where someone with a theorist's toolkit could actually contribute something right away. So I figured, worst case, I'd learn a lot about how these systems actually work, and I'd have some interesting stories to tell. That turned out to be true.

r001.rationale: It compares humans overseeing AI systems that outstrip them to a weak verifier interacting with a powerful, untrusted prover.

r002.rationale: It presents complexity theory’s verification work as a possible technical tool for AI oversight, while expressing skepticism about how much transfers.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me was the possibility that AI safety could involve precise mathematical questions where a complexity theorist could actually contribute. My first reaction was, you know, I care about this, but what do I know about making an AI safe? I’ve spent my career studying the capabilities and limitations of computation.

But one of the central questions is: how do you verify the work of a system that may be much more capable than you are? That has a very familiar flavor to a theoretical computer scientist. We study situations where finding an answer is hard, but checking it is easier. We study interactive proofs, where a computationally weak verifier can check claims made by a much more powerful prover.

Now, none of that automatically gives you a solution to AI alignment. The assumptions matter enormously, and checking a mathematical statement is different from checking whether a system is acting in your interests. But it suggested a way to turn at least some of these broad concerns into concrete research problems. That was the compelling part for me: there might be something useful here that draws on the tools I actually know.

r001.rationale: It compares verifying a much more capable system with a computationally weak verifier checking claims from a much more powerful prover.

r002.rationale: It says complexity-theory tools, including interactive proofs, could help turn AI safety concerns into concrete research problems.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, what appealed to me was the possibility of taking these very broad questions about AI safety and finding pieces of them that you could formulate precisely. What can you verify about a system’s behavior? What can you hide from a computationally bounded adversary? Where might cryptography give you a useful guarantee?

Complexity theory teaches you to be very careful about the assumptions behind a guarantee. A task might be possible in principle but completely infeasible computationally, and that distinction can matter enormously when you’re thinking about powerful AI systems.

That doesn’t mean complexity theory is going to solve alignment. But I found it compelling that there might be concrete problems where the tools I knew could actually contribute, rather than my just having opinions about the whole subject.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verifying system behavior and computationally bounded adversaries, but does not compare human oversight to a weak verifier checking a stronger, untrustworthy prover.

r002.rationale: It says broad AI safety questions may be made precise and asks what can be verified about a system, suggesting complexity theory tools could contribute to concrete AI safety problems.
